question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2022, urban geographer Halvard Tesmoor claimed that bicycle couriers with several years' experience in Dunvarrow reach unfamiliar delivery addresses faster than newly hired couriers do, because experienced couriers carry a more accurate overall picture of how the city's districts are laid out relative to one another.
• A team led by Annika Garrick at the Strand Hollow Transport Institute timed 30 experienced couriers (at least 5 years on the job) and 30 newly hired couriers (less than 6 months on the job) as each delivered to addresses that the courier had never visited before.
• The experienced couriers took an average of 14 minutes to reach an unfamiliar address; the newly hired couriers took an average of 23 minutes.
• The team also tested each of the same 60 couriers individually in a windowless room in the center of the city. For each of 12 well-known landmarks, one in each of the city's 12 districts, the courier turned a dial to point in the straight-line direction of that landmark, and the team recorded the angle of the dial.
• The team compared each courier's dial angles with the true compass directions to the landmarks and calculated the average pointing error in degrees.
• The average pointing error was 31 degrees for the experienced couriers and 31 degrees for the newly hired couriers.
• Delivery times were logged by each courier's handheld device, and the pointing sessions were held on weekday mornings.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Tesmoor's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings undermine Tesmoor's claim: the experienced couriers and the newly hired couriers had the same average pointing error in the windowless room, 31 degrees.
answer_b: The team's findings bear out Tesmoor's observation but not their explanation: the experienced couriers reached unfamiliar addresses in an average of 14 minutes to the newly hired couriers' 23 minutes, yet the two groups had the same average pointing error in the windowless room, 31 degrees.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Tesmoor's claim: the experienced couriers reached unfamiliar addresses in an average of 14 minutes, compared with an average of 23 minutes for the newly hired couriers.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Tesmoor's claim and show the two groups of couriers were otherwise comparable: the experienced couriers reached unfamiliar addresses in an average of 14 minutes to the newly hired couriers' 23 minutes, and both groups had the same average pointing error in the windowless room, 31 degrees.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it matches each part of Tesmoor's claim to the data that bears on it. Tesmoor's sentence says two things: that experienced couriers reach unfamiliar delivery addresses faster than newly hired couriers do, and that this happens because experienced couriers carry a more accurate overall picture of how the city's districts are laid out relative to one another. The delivery timing bears on the first part. The experienced couriers took an average of 14 minutes to reach an unfamiliar address, compared with 23 minutes for the newly hired couriers, so the faster deliveries Tesmoor described did appear. The pointing task bears on the second part. In a windowless room, a courier has no view of the surroundings to rely on, so turning a dial toward each landmark's straight-line direction depends on knowing where that landmark, and the district it stands in, lies in relation to the center of the city. Because there was one landmark in each of the 12 districts, a smaller average pointing error would indicate a more accurate understanding of how the districts are laid out relative to one another. The experienced and the newly hired couriers both had an average error of 31 degrees, so there was no sign that the experienced couriers hold a more accurate overall picture. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about how delivery times were logged and when the pointing sessions were held describe the method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The identical pointing errors (31 degrees for both groups) do count against Tesmoor's explanation about the couriers' overall knowledge of the city, but the claim also says that experienced couriers reach unfamiliar addresses faster, and the delivery times (14 versus 23 minutes) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 14 versus 23 minutes do fit the first part of Tesmoor's claim, that experienced couriers reach unfamiliar addresses faster, but Tesmoor also said this happens because experienced couriers have a more accurate overall picture of how the districts relate to one another, and the pointing results (31 degrees for both groups) show no such advantage. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the pointing result as a check on whether the groups were matched rather than as a test of the explanation. The pointing task asked couriers to indicate, without any view of the surroundings, the direction of a landmark in each of the city's 12 districts, which is the kind of knowledge Tesmoor's 'because' clause is about. The identical errors (31 degrees) therefore show that the two groups did not differ in that knowledge, which fails to support the explanation instead of confirming it. Nothing in the notes presents the pointing task as a way of showing that the groups were otherwise comparable. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism as added support for the claim.
